title: Part 1, Chapter 2
paragraphs: About the first sally the ingenious Don Quixote made from home

With these preliminaries settled, he wasn't about to put off his plan any longer, pushed on by the thought of how much the world was losing through his delay — given all the wrongs he meant to right, grievances to redress, injustices to repair, abuses to remove, and duties to discharge. So without telling anyone of his intention and without anyone seeing him, one morning before daybreak (on one of the hottest days of July) he put on his armour, mounted Rocinante with his patched-up helmet on his head, braced his shield, took up his lance, and rode out by the back gate of his yard onto the open plain — overjoyed and entirely satisfied to see how easily he had set his grand purpose in motion. But hardly had he reached the open ground when a terrible thought hit him — one that almost made him abandon the whole enterprise at the start. It occurred to him that he had never been formally dubbed a knight, and that under the law of chivalry he neither could nor should bear arms against any other knight; and that even if he had been dubbed, he ought, as a novice, to wear white armour with no device on his shield until he had earned one by his prowess. These reflections shook him, but his obsession was stronger than any reasoning, and he decided to have himself knighted by the first person he ran into, in line with the example of others in the same fix as he had read of in the books that had brought him to this point. As for the white armour, he resolved to scrub his at the first opportunity until it was whiter than an ermine; and with that reassurance he rode on, letting his horse pick the way, for he believed this was the essence of adventures.

So our newly minted adventurer made his way along, talking to himself: "Who knows but that in the days to come, when the true history of my famous deeds is published, the wise scholar who writes it, when he comes to set down my first sally in the early morning, will do it in this fashion? 'Scarcely had ruddy Apollo spread over the broad face of the earth the golden threads of his bright hair, scarcely had the little birds of painted plumage tuned their voices to greet with sweet and mellifluous harmony the coming of rosy Dawn — who, deserting the soft bed of her jealous husband, was showing herself to mortals at the gates and balconies of the Manchegan horizon — when the renowned knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, leaving the soft down behind, mounted his celebrated steed Rocinante and began to ride across the ancient and famous Campo de Montiel.'" Which in fact he was riding across. "Happy the age, happy the time," he went on, "in which my famous deeds shall be made known, worthy to be cast in bronze, carved in marble, painted in pictures, for a memorial forever. And you, O wise enchanter, whoever you may be, to whom it shall fall to be the chronicler of this strange history, do not, I beg you, forget my good Rocinante, the constant companion of all my travels." Then he broke out again, as if love-struck in earnest: "O Princess Dulcinea, lady of this captive heart, you have done me a terrible wrong to dismiss me with scorn and, by your harsh decree, banish me from the presence of your beauty. O lady, deign to remember this heart that is your vassal — that suffers such sorrow for love of you."

So he kept stringing together absurdities like this in the style his books had taught him, imitating their language as best he could, and meanwhile he rode so slowly and the sun climbed so quickly and beat down so fiercely that it would have been enough to melt his brains if he had any to melt. He travelled nearly all day without anything notable happening, which left him in despair, for he was anxious to encounter someone he could try the strength of his arm on.

There are writers who say his first adventure was the one at Puerto Lapice; others say it was the windmills. But what I have been able to establish, and find written in the annals of La Mancha, is that he was on the road all day, and towards nightfall both he and his horse were dead tired and starving. Looking around for some castle or shepherd's hut where he could refresh himself and ease his needs, he spotted an inn not far off the road — as welcome to him as a star guiding him to the gates, if not the palace, of his salvation; and he picked up the pace and reached it just as night was falling. At the door stood two young women, working girls (as they call them) on their way to Seville with some carriers who had stopped at the inn for the night; and since everything Don Quixote saw or thought of seemed to him to fit the books he'd read, the moment he saw the inn he pictured it as a castle with four turrets, pinnacles of polished silver, and the usual drawbridge, moat, and other castle furniture. Towards this inn, which to him was a castle, he advanced; and stopping Rocinante a short distance off, he waited for some dwarf to appear on the battlements and announce his arrival by sounding a trumpet. But when no one obliged and Rocinante was getting impatient for the stable, he rode up to the inn door and saw the two cheerful young women, who looked to him like two beautiful maidens or noble ladies taking the air at the gate of the castle.

Just then a swineherd, gathering his pigs from the stubble (and that is what they are called, with no apology), blew a blast on his horn to bring them together, and at once it seemed to Don Quixote to be exactly what he was expecting: some dwarf announcing his arrival. So with enormous satisfaction he rode up to the inn and the ladies, who, seeing a man approach in full armour with lance and shield, were starting to retreat into the inn in fright when Don Quixote — guessing their alarm from their flight — raised his pasteboard visor, revealed his dry, dusty face, and addressed them in a courteous tone: "Your ladyships need not run away or fear any rudeness, for the order of knighthood I profess does not permit me to offer any to anyone, least of all to high-born maidens of the kind your appearance proclaims you to be." The girls were staring, trying to make out his features behind the clumsy visor; but when they heard themselves called maidens, which was so far from their actual line of work, they could not keep from laughing. That made Don Quixote indignant, and he said, "Modesty becomes the fair, and what's more, laughter with no real cause behind it is great silliness. But I do not say this to hurt or anger you, for my one desire is to be of service."

The incomprehensible language and unpromising look of our knight only made the girls laugh harder, which made him angrier, and things might have got out of hand if the innkeeper had not come out at that moment. He was a very fat man and therefore a very peaceful one. He, seeing this grotesque figure in armour that matched none of its parts — saddle, bridle, lance, shield, or breastplate — was not at all inclined to join the girls in their laughter; but, in fact, a little nervous of so much hardware, he thought it wise to speak smoothly, so he said, "Señor Caballero, if your worship is looking for a room — bed apart, since there is none in the inn — we have plenty of everything else here." Don Quixote, noting the respectful manner of the Alcaide of the fortress (so the innkeeper and inn seemed to him), replied, "Sir Castellan, anything will do for me, for
'My armour is my only wear, my only rest the fray.'"

The host imagined he was being called Castellan because he took him for a worthy Castilian, though he was in fact an Andalusian from the beach at Sanlúcar — as crafty a thief as Cacus and as full of tricks as a student or a page. "In that case," said he,
"'Your bed is on the flinty rock, your sleep to watch alway;'

and if so, you can dismount and count on plenty of sleeplessness under this roof for a twelvemonth, never mind a single night." Saying this, he stepped over to hold the stirrup for Don Quixote, who dismounted with great difficulty and effort (he hadn't eaten all day), and then asked his host to take good care of his horse, which was the finest piece of horseflesh that ever ate bread in this world. The innkeeper looked Rocinante over and did not find him anywhere near as good as Don Quixote said, nor half as good; and after putting him in the stable, he came back to see what his guest wanted. By now the girls had made their peace with Don Quixote and were helping him off with his armour. They had taken off his breastplate and backpiece, but they didn't know how to undo his gorget or remove his makeshift helmet, which he had tied on with green ribbons whose knots were so tangled they would have to be cut. This Don Quixote refused absolutely to allow, so he kept his helmet on all evening, the strangest and drollest figure imaginable. While they relieved him of the rest of his armour, he took the cheap pair who were doing it for ladies of high rank in the castle, and addressed them, sprightly as ever:
"Oh, never, surely, was there knight so served by hand of dame as served was he, Don Quixote hight, when from his town he came; with maidens waiting on himself, princesses on his hack —

— or Rocinante, for that, ladies, is my horse's name, and Don Quixote of La Mancha my own. I had no intention of declaring myself until my deeds in your service and honour had announced me, but the need to adapt that old ballad of Lancelot to the present occasion has given you my name a little prematurely. There will, however, be a time when your ladyships will command and I will obey, and then the strength of my arm will show how much I wish to serve you."

The girls were not used to this kind of rhetoric and had no reply; they only asked if he wanted something to eat. "I would happily eat something," said Don Quixote, "for I feel it would come at a useful moment." The day happened to be a Friday, and the only food in the entire inn was some pieces of the fish that is called in Castile _abadejo_, in Andalusia _bacallao_, in some places _curadillo_, and in others _troutlet_; so they asked if he could manage troutlet, since they had nothing else to offer. "If there are enough troutlets," said Don Quixote, "they will come to the same thing as a trout, for it's all one to me whether I am given eight reals in small change or a single piece of eight; and besides, these troutlets may be like veal — better than beef — or kid, which is better than goat. Whatever it is, let it come quickly, for the weight and labour of arms cannot be borne without support to the inside." They set up a table for him at the door of the inn, for the air, and the innkeeper brought him a portion of poorly soaked and worse cooked stockfish and a piece of bread as black and mouldy as his armour. It was a laughable sight to see him eat, for with his helmet on and the beaver up, he could not put anything into his mouth with his own hands; someone else had to feed him, and one of the ladies did that. To give him anything to drink would have been impossible, had the landlord not bored out a reed, put one end in his mouth, and poured the wine through the other — all of which Don Quixote endured rather than have the ribbons of his helmet cut.

While this was going on, a hog-gelder came up to the inn and announced his arrival with four or five blasts on his reed pipe — which completely convinced Don Quixote that he was in some famous castle and that they were entertaining him with music, that the stockfish was trout, the bread the whitest wheat, the working girls noble ladies, and the innkeeper the castellan of the castle. He concluded that his enterprise and his first sally had been worth the trouble. But it still distressed him that he had not yet been formally dubbed a knight, since it was clear he could not lawfully take on any adventure without first receiving the order of knighthood.
